openers.evidence-risks-and-greenwashing: Not every green promise holds up. This chapter looks at the gap between claim and reality, starting with advertising meant to make products, goals or policies look good for the environment. It turns to farming and forestry that grow a single species at a time, and to the trees planted to pull carbon dioxide from the air. A subtle physical effect complicates that hope: dark forest canopies absorb more sunlight, partly cancelling the cooling that stored carbon brings. Rules on what businesses may claim, and lists of common deceptions, are the tools for telling real benefit from spin.

nature-nbs-075.title: Greenwashing: selling a green image instead of green action
nature-nbs-075.text: In 1986 New York environmentalist Jay Westerveld noticed hotels urging guests to reuse towels to 'save the environment'. The main effect was lower laundry costs. His essay coined a word blending 'green' with 'whitewashing'. Greenwashing is advertising or public relations meant to mislead people into believing an organization's products, goals or policies are good for the environment. Firms do it to win legitimacy with environmentally minded people, to look responsible to the wider public, and to distance themselves from their own or their suppliers' failings. A common rule of thumb: an organization is greenwashing if it spends far more on advertising a green image than on acting in environmentally sound ways. The practice is widespread. A 2020 European Union study found over 50% of examined environmental claims were vague, misleading or unfounded, and 40% were unsubstantiated. Many companies pledged net-zero emissions after the 2015 Paris Agreement, but critics say their plans are unfeasible rather than real cuts. With no agreed definition, consumers and regulators can struggle to call a case. Critics argue that widespread greenwashing, with weak enforcement, makes consumers doubt all green claims. That weakens their power to push firms toward greener practices.

nature-nbs-082.title: Monoculture: one crop, one field, short-term gains
nature-nbs-082.text: Over 600 million liters of pesticides are sprayed each year after pest outbreaks. Many of those outbreaks trace back to monoculture, growing a single crop species in a field at a time. In the short term it is easy and efficient: uniform planting, care and harvest often give higher yields and lower costs. With synthetic fertilizers, it has reduced the extra land needed for food, which is called land sparing. Over the long term, though, monocultures are more prone to disease and pests, because local biodiversity falls and nutrients run down. Perennial monocultures such as oil palm, sugarcane, tea and pines can acidify and degrade soils. Declining soil health leads to more fertilizer, whose excess nitrogen can contaminate drinking water and feed algal blooms. Diversity can be added through crop rotation, intercropping, agroecology, silvopasture and mixed-species plantations.

nature-nbs-090.title: Albedo: how much sunlight a surface throws back
nature-nbs-090.text: Fresh snow reflects about 0.9 to 0.95 of visible light. Charcoal reflects about 0.04. That share of incoming sunlight a surface reflects is its albedo. It runs from 0, a black body absorbing everything, to 1, a surface reflecting everything. Oceans and most forests have low albedo, while deserts are among the most reflective landforms. Deciduous trees score about 0.15 to 0.18, conifers about 0.09 to 0.15. Albedo shapes climate by setting how much radiation a planet absorbs. So land-use changes such as deforestation, farming and urbanization, which alter albedo, can perturb Earth's energy balance.

nature-nbs-087.title: Tree planting: putting seedlings in the ground
nature-nbs-087.text: Planted forests covered an estimated 312 million ha in 2025, 8% of all forest area, after growing by 120 million ha since 1990. Tree planting is transplanting young seedlings into the ground, usually for forestry, land reclamation or landscaping. Done properly it can regenerate a deforested area, but a planted forest rarely matches the biodiversity and complexity of a natural one. Outside interests often profit more from fast-growing species such as eucalyptus or pine. Their plantations bring far smaller biodiversity benefits than native forest and are often controversial as carbon offsets. Almost all plantation forests (95%) in South America are of introduced species. Many environmentalists argue that only native trees should be planted. Planting can even harm biodiversity, especially in tropical savannas.

nature-nbs-098.title: Tree plantations: forests built to produce wood
nature-nbs-098.text: In 2000, plantations made up 5% of global forest but supplied an estimated 35% of the world's roundwood. A tree plantation is a forest planted to produce large volumes of wood, usually as a single-species monoculture. Managed timber forests commonly yield 1 to 3 cubic meters of wood per hectare per year. Fast-growing plantations commonly yield 20 to 30 or more. Industrial ones are large, even-aged blocks of one or two species, often bred for fast growth. Eucalyptus is the most widely planted tree. Fiber farms, started in Brazil in the 1970s, run on rotations as short as 5 to 15 years. Most trees are cut after 10 to 60 years, so plantations lack old-growth's soil, wildlife and dead wood. They offer local people far fewer services than the forest they replace. Their long-term carbon storage depends on what happens to the harvested wood.

nature-nbs-079.title: Policing green claims: rules against greenwashing
nature-nbs-079.text: A January 2021 European Commission review found green claims on 42 percent of consumer websites examined were likely false and misleading. Rules on such claims differ worldwide, from criminal liability to fines to voluntary guidelines. The US Federal Trade Commission's voluntary 'green guides' say any qualifications must be clear, prominent and understandable. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority published a Green Claims Code in September 2021. In June 2024 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled that firms advertising as 'climate neutral' must define the term. EU rules require companies with over 250 staff and €40 million turnover to disclose ESG information. Firms may also seek certification so independent checks verify their claims.

nature-nbs-084.title: Forest monocultures: carbon gains, local losses
nature-nbs-084.text: In China, a shift to cheap plantings of mostly red pine meant trees died before delivering their expected carbon offset. Forest monocultures are plantations of a single tree species, often grown for timber. After deforestation, single-species afforestation has become popular for carbon sequestration. Eucalyptus, pines and acacias are common in the tropics and Global South, often imported species replacing native forest. Such schemes may help the global climate yet cause local harm, including soil depletion and altered water cycles. They reduce biodiversity and weaken resistance to pests and disease. They offer few local jobs, and profits follow a boom-and-bust pattern rarely reinvested in the land.

nature-nbs-091.title: The forest albedo trade-off: carbon versus darkness
nature-nbs-091.text: Forests look dark from above because they absorb most ultraviolet and visible light for photosynthesis. That darkness creates a trade-off. Dark canopies absorb more sunlight, partly cancelling the cooling gained when new trees store carbon. Location decides which effect wins. In snowy regions, treeless winter albedo is 10% to 50% higher than nearby forest, because snow does not cover trees as readily. For snowy evergreen forests, the effect can be large enough that clearing them causes net cooling. Hadley Centre studies found new tropical and midlatitude forests tended to cool. High-latitude forests, such as in Siberia, were neutral or perhaps warming. A 2023 study of 176 flux stations found afforestation may cause moderate warming for about 20 years before turning to significant cooling. Tropical reforestation helps form clouds that reflect sunlight. Boreal reforestation swaps bright snow for dark canopy and helps less. Trees also release water vapor, which is usually treated as net cooling. So the overall effect depends heavily on local climate.

nature-nbs-088.title: Planting trees to fight climate change: promise and limits
nature-nbs-088.text: Forests take up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year. Using new trees to pull carbon dioxide from the air and store it is an obvious idea for limiting climate change. Forests can switch roles, though. In 2019 they absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of heat, drought and deforestation. Avoiding deforestation beats clearing and replanting. Clearing causes irreversible biodiversity loss and soil damage, and new forests take several decades to deliver comparable carbon benefits. Scientists call protecting and restoring carbon-rich, long-lived ecosystems, especially natural forests, 'the major climate solution'. One estimate found room for 0.9 billion ha more tree canopy, and it has been criticized as far too high. Counting albedo and other feedbacks, the area that truly cools is 20-80% lower. That planting would store 205 billion tons of carbon only if the trees survive future climate stress to maturity. The carbon must also not return to the air when trees burn or rot. Mixed-species plantations would store more than single-species ones.

nature-nbs-078.title: Greenscamming: green names for anti-green groups
nature-nbs-078.text: Openly arguing for environmental damage is hard when protection enjoys broad public support. So some groups hide behind a name. Greenscamming is giving an organization or product a name that falsely suggests it is environmentally friendly. Industrial firms use such front groups to dispute science that threatens their business, such as fossil energy companies denying human-caused warming. ExxonMobil supported more than 100 climate denial organizations and spent about 20 million U.S. dollars on greenscamming groups.

nature-nbs-076.title: The seven sins of greenwashing
nature-nbs-076.text: By 2010, about 95% of U.S. consumer products claiming to be green committed at least one sin, TerraChoice reported. In 2007 the consultancy listed seven: hidden trade-off, no proof, vagueness, worshipping false labels, irrelevance, lesser of two evils, and fibbing. A hidden trade-off calls a product green on a narrow set of attributes while ignoring bigger issues. The United Nations lists similar tactics, such as announcing future milestones without real plans.

nature-nbs-077.title: Types of greenwashing: where the deception starts
nature-nbs-077.text: Greenwashing can be sorted by where the deception arises. Direct greenwashing is when a firm's own processes contradict its claims. Indirect greenwashing is when a supplier's false claims harm the firm it supplies. Vicarious greenwashing blames a green firm for its polluting partner. At product level, 'claim' greenwashing uses misleading labels such as 'eco-friendly', while 'executional' greenwashing relies on green colors and nature imagery.

nature-nbs-085.title: Agro-extractivism: farming for export, controlled from abroad
nature-nbs-085.text: More than 46 million hectares of soy have been planted in South America, and over half a million hectares are deforested each year for cultivation. Agro-extractivism is foreign control over farming, driven by large-scale export commodities often grown as monocultures. These have reduced local and indigenous food sovereignty, food security and access to land and water. Repeated single cropping exhausts soil nutrients and microbes, increasing reliance on synthetic fertilizers.

nature-nbs-083.title: Genetic monoculture: when every plant is the same
nature-nbs-083.text: Ireland relied on a single potato variety, the 'lumper'. When Phytophthora infestans arrived, the result was the Great Famine of 1845–1849. Genetic monoculture is planting crops, or raising animals, with little or no genetic variation across a region. One disease they cannot resist can wipe out entire crops. Gros Michel bananas, all clones, fell to Fusarium wilt, and growers switched to the Cavendish by the early 1960s. It faces similar risk, and genetic sameness threatens food security.

nature-nbs-086.title: Mixed-species plantations: more species, more value
nature-nbs-086.text: A tree plantation need not be one species. Mixed-species plantations grow several together. Several studies show well-managed ones earn more from timber than monocultures. They also store more carbon and hold more biodiversity. They remain less common because of a mistaken belief that they cost more and are harder to manage.

nature-nbs-093.title: How cities and farms change Earth's brightness
nature-nbs-093.text: Urban areas are commonly 0.01–0.02 lower in albedo than nearby cropland, which adds to warming. Human land use such as cities, farms and deforestation changes how much sunlight land reflects. The change can also be turned around on purpose. Raising urban albedo can ease the urban heat island effect. A 2022 estimate found that raising albedo by 0.1 across the world's cities would cool as much as absorbing ~44 Gt of CO2.

nature-nbs-092.title: The ice-albedo feedback: melting that feeds itself
nature-nbs-092.text: Fresh snow has an albedo of about 0.9, melting snow about 0.4 and dirty snow about 0.2. The ice-albedo feedback is a self-reinforcing loop. Melting snow or ice exposes darker surfaces, which absorb more heat and cause more melting. As Arctic ice melts, darker water and ground reflect less heat back to space. It is one of the main reinforcing climate feedbacks, with water vapor and the net effect of clouds.

nature-nbs-097.title: When systematic reviews mislead
nature-nbs-097.text: Systematic reviews are treated as the strongest evidence, yet they can mislead. A 2003 review of 300 studies found they were not all equally reliable. Of 100 reviews monitored, 7% needed updating on publication, another 4% within a year and another 11% within 2 years. Around half of clinical trials never report results, and 'positive' trials were twice as likely to be published. Many reviews also report poorly and use weak, hard-to-reproduce searches.

nature-nbs-096.title: Scoping reviews: mapping what evidence exists
nature-nbs-096.text: Before a full review, researchers often ask whether one is even possible. A scoping review maps the concepts, language and data around a topic, refining its search as it goes. It gauges how much evidence an area holds and often comes before a systematic review. Its methods may change during the work. A related mapping review sorts literature by quantity, quality and study design to show where research is needed.

nature-nbs-100.title: Introduced species in plantations
nature-nbs-100.text: Globally, 44 percent of plantation forests are made up mainly of introduced species, trees planted far outside their natural range. Pine, spruce and eucalyptus are classic examples, valued for fast growth and tolerance of degraded farmland. The share varies by region. Introduced species dominate in South America (88%), Oceania (75%) and East and Southern Africa (65%). They are only 1%, 3% and 8% in North America, West and Central Asia, and Europe.

nature-nbs-099.title: Do plantations spare natural forests or replace them?
nature-nbs-099.text: In New Zealand, 19% of the forest area supplies 99% of industrial roundwood. Foresters say high-yield plantations like these need less land and so spare natural forests. In practice some replace them. About 15% of plantations in tropical countries are set up on closed-canopy natural forest. Still, the FAO finds only about 7% of tropical natural forest lost goes to plantations, and 93% to agriculture and other uses. Their carbon benefit is also challenged, since the CO2 is eventually released after harvest.

nature-nbs-080.title: Bluewashing: greenwashing for the oceans
nature-nbs-080.text: Bluewashing is a term closely akin to greenwashing. It means false or misleading claims about how an action affects water and ocean environments. The term comes up in discussions of the blue economy, the sustainable development of coastal and ocean resources.

reviews.evidence-risks-and-greenwashing: Green claims are everywhere, and many do not survive scrutiny: by 2010 about 95% of U.S. products claiming to be green committed at least one of the seven sins. Tree planting shows how a real benefit can be oversold. Single-species plantations, often of introduced trees, store less carbon and hold less wildlife than mixed or natural forests. Dark canopies absorb sunlight, so new forests in snowy regions may help the climate little or even warm it. Rules on green claims and careful reviews of evidence are the tools for separating genuine benefit from spin.
